newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iranian leaders weigh response to U.S. overtures.
newsitem.headline: Iranian leaders weigh response to U.S. overtures.

text.p: Iranian leaders are locked in debate over how to respond to overtures for dialogue with their declared enemy the United States.

European diplomats in Tehran engaged in an EU policy of critical dialogue with Iran are excited by what they detect as change in the U.S. attitude: isolation may not be the best policy towards the largest power in the oil-rich Gulf.
"We sense change coming from the think tanks in Washington, the opposition and some American media," one diplomat said.
Tehran and Washington have been stuck in a generation of enmity since the 1979 Islamic revolution toppled Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, a close U.S. ally.
Religious leaders including supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and Majlis (parliament) speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri still refer to the United States as "the Great Satan".
"Death to America", a trade mark of the revolution, was chanted by crowds in Tehran only last week at rallies marking the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the U.S. embassy.

Nateq-Nouri, tipped as a possible successor next year to President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, told crowds outside the former U.S. embassy: "...America is a blood-sucking wolf who was slapped in the face by us on this historic day. There can never be a friendly relationship between a lamb and a wolf."
But others in the Islamic republic's capital appear more open to prospects of contacts with Washington.
Rafsanjani said last week Tehran's policy since the time of the late spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini had been to demand an end to Washington's anti-Iran stand.
"It is America's own fault. If they calm down, as the Imam (Khomeini) put it, there are no problems from our side. The leader's (Khamenei's) present policy is the same and I also follow this line."

Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati, in a further sign of openness, said on Sunday: "If they (the United States) send a message to us through their interest section (at the Swiss embassy), it will not remain unanswered.
"In case of necessity, it will be replied through our interest section (at the Pakistani embassy) in Washington," he told reporters in Tehran.

Interest sections in third-country embassies have looked after Iranian and American affairs in each other's countries since 1980 when Washington severed diplomatic relations over the seizure of its embassy in Tehran by Moslem militants who held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau said in Dubai last month the lack of dialogue was unsatisfactory and Washington wanted talks with Tehran on bilateral differences.
"The problem in dealing with Iran is that there are competing power centres in Tehran," a Gulf-based diplomat said. "There are bound to be contradictions."

From the seizure of the hostages during the administration of President Jimmy Carter to trade and investment sanctions imposed by President Bill Clinton, the atmosphere between the two antagonists has remained poisoned.
The two countries disagree fervently about everything from the U.S.-brokered Middle East peace process to the post-Cold War world order and the impact of Western culture on Asian nations.

Iran, with more than 60 million people, is the Gulf's most populous nation by far. While U.S. companies have been frozen out of the Iranian market by the sanctions, European countries have continued dialogue and lucrative business.
The United States seeks to isolate Iran and punish it economically for what it calls state sponsorship of terrorism and for seeking to acquire weapons of mass destruction.
Iran, in turn, accuses the United States of attempting to topple its Islamic government and establish U.S. hegemony over the strategic region through a huge military presence.

The Pentagon says U.S. warships and warplanes are there to protect the unhindered flow of Gulf oil to world markets at stable prices, which it describes as the paramount U.S. national security interest in the region.
